title: How the NEP’s killing of the public university brought Gen Z out on the streets
author: Eram Agha
image_caption: Student protesters carry a portrait of Jotirao and Savitribai Phule as they march towards parliament, on 20 July 2026. Nearly every student had some story of an ugly clash with India’s costly, bureaucratic and ultimately crumbling higher education system in the last five years.Shahid Tantray for The Caravan
content_html:
{ONE}

GROWING UP IN THE 2000s, I hated the prospect of sitting for competitive entrance examinations. I only ever sat for two, and the entire process—studying for days under a cloud of anxiety, the nervous energy of those exam halls—made me want to bypass the process and enter the workforce early. Unlike my two sisters, I was not a very bright student. Luckily, getting into a government college in Lucknow was not a problem. We were admitted based on our twelfth-standard marks, and I just had to fill a form. Avadh Girls Degree College was only seven kilometres from my home. Later, my undergraduate marks were enough to get me into a master’s degree in political science in the same university. When I became a journalist, working in several of the city’s newspapers, one of my main beats was covering education. I had a chance to report from university towns such as Aligarh, before seeing how it worked in Delhi.

Things have changed drastically since my student days. With nearly every student interview I conducted over the past six months for this story, I found that the landscape had become so challenging that I feel certain, had I been dealt the same institutional cards, I would simply not have made it through the hoops the youth of today have to jump through.

Nearly forty percent of India’s 1.4 billion population is under the age of 25. To serve them, the higher-education department counts 52,397 colleges managed by 1,422 universities. The bulk of these are state-level public and private universities. State governments still account for about ninety percent of budget expenditure on education. This makes sense, because states whose demography and literacy levels are as starkly different as Kerala and Bihar need different education solutions.

title: The government’s harmful gatekeeping of gender-affirming healthcare
author: Ananta Jain
image_caption: At Bengaluru’s Freedom Park, people from the transgender community, activists and allies hold placards during a protest, held on 18 March 2026, against the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill ahead of its discussion in parliament.Idrees Mohammed / AFP / Getty Images
content_html:
The fundamental rights of transgender and intersex persons received a severe blow early this year, with the passage of The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Act, 2026. The amendments effectively nullified the right to self-determination and self-identification of gender, and severely restrict other fundamental rights of trans persons, guaranteed by a 2014 judgement of the Supreme Court in NALSA vs The Union of India. The Narendra Modi government proposed the amendments on 13 March and rammed them through both houses of parliament within three days. They received President Draupadi Murmu’s assent on 30 March. Throughout the process, the union ministry of social justice and empowerment swept aside consultations with trans and intersex persons, as well as widespread objection to the proposed law by both these communities and other gender minorities.

Indian law now imposes the mandatory examination of individuals by a medical board—which will “verify” their gender—and the invasive scrutiny of their private medical records by public officials as prerequisites for the legal recognition of transgender persons. On the other hand, the vague wording of the law risks criminalising individuals and organisations that provide material support, logistical aid and shelter, or medical help to trans persons. Crucially, the amended legal definition of a transgender person includes only “a person having such socio-cultural identities as kinner, hijra, aravani and jogta, or eunuch” or “a person with intersex variations specified” by the new law, or “a person who, at birth, has a congenital variation.” In addition to unscientifically conflating transgender identity with intersex genetic variations, this extremely narrow definition excludes persons who identify with or express transmasculine, non-binary and genderqueer identities, as well as socioculturally recognised gender minorities, such as nupi-manbi and -manba, thirunangai–thirunambi, khwajasira, kothi and others, who had legal recognition under the 2019 act. The new law not only pushes the transgender and intersex communities’ advocacy for rights and protections many steps backwards but also entrenches an unscientific, prejudiced and thoroughly outdated biological framework to understand gender.

The amendments have triggered a public-health emergency, according to Dr Sanjay Sharma, the founder of the Association for Transgender Health in India. Despite the Modi government’s rush in parliament, it has yet to issue the amended rules or any further guidelines to be followed by institutions meant to serve individuals who have or are seeking to transition medically, through gender-affirming medical procedures, and legally, by securing documentation that accurately records their gender and chosen name. Many intracommunity groups, both online and offline, are seeing messages seeking clarity on existing procedures for medical and legal transitions, or help in navigating new procedures, and are witnessing charged discussions about what the stripping of legal protections for a large section of trans persons portends. “It feels like a nightmare,” Koyel Ghosh, the managing trustee of Sappho For Equality, a Kolkata-based non-governmental organisation supporting queer women and transmasculine persons, told me. Calls to SFE’s crisis helpline have increased since the legal amendments, Ghosh added. “There’s a mental-health epidemic where people are feeling extremely suicidal.”

“We also need to understand that we are talking about a group of people who have been marginalised and ostracised by the society,” Sharma told me. Given that science, law and society continue to invisibilise gender variance and transgender identity, most people in the community have, in Sharma’s words, “very poor health-seeking behaviour.” Many of the individuals I spoke to barely discussed their visits to doctors—even for general health check-ups—since every encounter comes with scrutiny, adverse judgement and the invasion of privacy. “There is a lot of hesitation we feel just approaching hospitals and doctors in general,” John, a trans man in his twenties who is based in Kolkata, told me. “Any trans person needs to worry if a doctor is being enabled to ask for more documentation, or if any doctor is being enabled by their medical directors or by medical review boards to make things more complicated,” he added. “Because things are already complicated. Things are already inaccessible.”

title: What the Jantar Mantar protests made clear
author: Shahid Tantray
content_html:
Neha Bora, a doctoral student, is the president of the All India Students Association, which is affiliated with the Communist Party of India (Marxist–Leninist) (Liberation). During the recent student protests at Jantar Mantar—which culminated in the resignation of the union education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan—Bora carried out a 23-day hunger strike alongside two other AISA activists and the Ladakhi educationist Sonam Wangchuk.

The movement emerged from the massive popularity of the Cockroach Janata Party, a satirical social-media platform started by Abhijeet Dipke, a 30-year-old who had previously worked with the Aam Aadmi Party and was studying in the United States. In early June, Dipke returned to India, and the CJP called for protests. The protesters’ demands coalesced around education, especially the leak of the examination papers for the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test held earlier this year, which was then cancelled. At least twelve students took their lives in the aftermath of the cancellation. Student organisations such as AISA, the Students’ Federation of India and the All India Students’ Federation provided crucial support in organising the agitation. The CJP demanded Pradhan’s resignation and compensation for the deceased students’ families. The student groups also called attention to the Narendra Modi government’s educational policies, opposing the formation of the National Testing Agency and the implementation of the National Educational Policy, 2020. Videos of the protests, including memes and reels criticising and mocking the government, went viral for days on platforms such as Instagram.

The CJP protests swelled after the police forcibly removed Wangchuk from the site and later cracked down on young people who continued to protest in massive numbers. As one of the student leaders of the protests, Bora has become a prominent face of the youth movement. Shahid Tantray, a multimedia reporter at The Caravan, spoke to them several times over the course of the agitation, when they were on a hunger strike, as well as after Pradhan’s resignation.

What was your first reaction when you heard Dharmendra Pradhan resigned? What does it mean in the broader political context, especially given Prime Minister Narendra Modi has rarely accepted ministerial resignations under public pressure?

title: The Ram Mandir donations theft and Modi’s men who should answer for it
author: Dhirendra K Jha,Amrita Singh
image_caption: Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya, Uttar Pradesh, on 25 November 2025.Press Information Bureau/ Andolu/ Getty Images
content_html:
FIVE MONTHS AFTER Narendra Modi began his second term as prime minister, the Supreme Court delivered his government a momentous gift. On 9 November 2019, it settled a land dispute in Ayodhya, stretching back over a century, in favour of the Hindu Right. The push to build a Ram Mandir was at the political centre of a decades-long fight for the soul of India—a struggle whose most violent chapter was the 1992 demolition of the Babri Masjid, one of the most egregious acts of communal vandalism in independent India’s history.

Despite a token acknowledgment that the mosque’s destruction by a Hindu mob had been a criminal act, the judgment was a massive symbolic victory for the Bharatiya Janata Party. It was proof that the party could deliver on the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh’s dream of a Hindu Rashtra. The court mandated the union government to set up a trust within three months to oversee the construction of the temple. On the face of it, this was meant to be neither a government body nor an extension of the ruling party. But what it was going to be was that the Sangh would become the custodian of one of the most politically charged religious institutions in modern India, receiving land, donations and extraordinary public trust.

Modi announced the formation of the trust in parliament, on 5 February 2020, framing the issue as a “very important and historical subject for the country” and declaring that the trust would “be fully autonomous to take any decision regarding the construction of the temple.” The Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra would be staffed with 15 members, including the magistrate or district collector of Ayodhya and representatives of the union and Uttar Pradesh governments—with the trust deed explicitly instructing that members must be “practising Hindus.” The rest of the trustees were drawn from various monastic orders. Many of those presented as independent figures had been key in sustaining the Ram Mandir campaign or were bureaucrats who had been influential in various projects of the Sangh.

title: Contemporary fiction about the internet
author: Saachi Gupta
content_html:
FIVE YEARS AGO, the editor Emily Temple pointed to a conspicuous gap in literature at the time. “Relative to the amount of space it takes up in the collective and capitalist imagination, the internet has had less of an impact on contemporary fiction than one might expect,” she wrote. “It is increasingly acknowledged in novels but it seems oddly difficult to represent well.” One can speculate about the many reasons why this might have been the case: social class restricting access to the internet, or authors not having much of a reference point while sketching out social media’s minute intricacies. In her book Never Logged Out: How the Internet Created India’s Gen Z, Ria Chopra observes that “digital platforms are built to support writing about digital experience.” It is possible, for instance, to hyperlink references, embed or edit posts to corroborate claims or respond to developments, but the dynamic nature of the internet means it “resists portrayal in any medium other than itself.” To write about it is no doubt daunting—after all, the web is no longer just a means of escaping reality but a parallel universe in itself, complete with its own languages, subcultures, currencies and social hierarchies.

Published late last year, Chopra’s book is one of many recent attempts by South Asian women to articulate their experience of existing on the internet. In the last year, other works of non-fiction—Vauhini Vora’s Searches and Sukhnidh Kaur’s Your Perfect Dream Girl: Influencers, AI, and the Future of Desire—also study the dread users have been expressing about certain aspects of the internet, particularly with artificial intelligence now added in the mix. In the burgeoning fiction about the same theme, meanwhile, two features seem constant: a seemingly self-aware first-person narrator unable to break out of destructive patterns, and a sense of mounting anxiety as the consequences of their online interactions start to bleed into their offline lives.

One of the most ambitious in this catalogue is Meena Kandasamy’s new novel Fieldwork as a Sex Object, in which a scandalous deepfake video of the protagonist suddenly goes viral. Overnight, Amrita—“Amy”—Chaturvedi becomes a trending hashtag, embroiled first in a media frenzy and then a vicious legal battle, shunned by friends and family, persecuted by right-wing trolls and left-wing puritans alike. “The main aggressors are a disparate bunch of Nazi-loving, Islamophobic vegetarian dicks with profile pictures that are either the Joker or V for Vendetta,” she scoffs. “If these trolls are to be believed, I am a leading member of the tukde-tukde gang of academics who want to balkanise India. I am on Pakistani payroll. I am funded by George Soros.”

Meanwhile, Amy gets flak from others for not being woke enough. “They claim offence because I apparently retweeted, a long, long time ago, that the porn industry should be banned,” she explains, adding that someone on X is doing a multipart thread on “how ethical, homemade, organic, fairtrade porn helped them embrace their own sexuality. No, it is not a parody.” When a single user finally jumps to her defence, it is because of Amy’s caste privilege. “Ms Chaturvedi has been targeted because she is a Brahmin,” tweets @DesiInNYC, incensing both Amy and Nimmi, her only ally through this ordeal, who is Dalit. By embodying this polarisation, and the fast-paced chaos, Kandasamy’s novel reckons with how conversations tend to unravel on social media. Like other recent books, it approaches the subject of the internet not as a vast, complex, interconnected network but instead from the inside, through the singular experience of someone who is a victim of Big Tech, aware of their addiction yet unable to extricate themselves from it.
